title: 1 MW data center site: where to find powered space for a 1 MW load in the US
description: Find a 1 MW data center site in the US: energized edge, inference and mining sites, what 1 MW really fits, the service you need and how fast it can be live.
intro: A 1 MW data center site is the easiest size to find and the easiest to get wrong. At this scale you are almost always on the utility distribution system, so the fastest sites are buildings or yards that already have the service in place. A new 1 MW service can take longer than people expect because of transformer lead times and feeder upgrades. Invariant keeps a running list of energized small sites across the US, from 0.5 MW turnkey mining yards to Tier III rooms, and shares the ones that fit on a call.
takeaways: 1 MW at the meter is about 0.77 MW of IT at an assumed facility-to-IT demand ratio of 1.30. That is roughly six 120 kW AI racks, or a few hundred air-cooled mining machines.
At this size the question is the existing service: voltage, transformer rating and whether the feeder has room. A site that already has it can be live in weeks.
Land is rarely the issue. A containerized 1 MW deployment fits on well under an acre.
Ask for a recent utility bill or a service letter showing the transformer and the contracted capacity, not a map of nearby lines.

sections.heading: What 1 MW actually fits

blocks.text: The utility serves total facility load, including cooling and electrical losses. Confirm the simultaneous loads at the site’s design conditions. At an assumed facility-to-IT demand ratio of 1.30, a 1 MW site leaves about 0.77 MW for IT. At about 120 kW per NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 rack, that is six full racks, or 432 GPUs, before reserving power for other IT equipment. Air-cooled designs at 30 to 50 kW per rack fit more racks and fewer GPUs per MW. Typical buyers at this size are edge inference, a small GPU pod, enterprise compute or a bitcoin mining deployment.

Utility distribution service. Usually a pad-mounted transformer stepping a 12 to 35 kV feeder down to 480 V, sometimes primary service at the feeder voltage.
Under 1 acre for containers; a small warehouse or retrofit room for a built facility.
Weeks if the service exists. New service can run from a few months to more than a year where transformers or feeder work are on order.
Recent utility bills, the service agreement or contract demand, the transformer nameplate, and a note from the utility on any headroom above the current load.

blocks.text: These ranges are Invariant’s working figures from sites we have screened. They are not published standards, and individual utilities and designs land outside them.

sections.heading: Where 1 MW sites come from

blocks.text: Most 1 MW sites we see are one of four things: a light industrial building with a large existing service, a small mining yard with containers already wired, a room inside a colocation facility, or a spot inside the fence of a power plant or industrial user that has spare capacity on its own transformers.

Each has a different catch. Industrial buildings often have the amps but not the cooling. Mining yards have power and airflow but no redundancy. Colocation rooms are fast and expensive per kW. Plant sites can be the cheapest power you will ever see, with the least flexibility on hours and terms.

sections.heading: What to check before you sign

blocks.text: Confirm the contracted capacity on the bill, not the panel rating. A building with a 4,000 A switchboard at 480 V can in theory carry more than 3 MW, yet its utility contract and transformer may cap it far lower.
Ask whether the power is firm or interruptible. Many small mining sites run on curtailable rates. That suits miners and does not suit an inference customer with an uptime promise.

title: 5 MW data center site: finding energized power for a 5 MW load in the US
description: Find a 5 MW data center site in the US: turnkey energized sites, how many racks 5 MW fits, the feeder and transformer you need and how long new service takes.
intro: 5 MW is where a data center site stops being a building with a big service and starts needing its own utility plan. A 5 MW load is usually still on a distribution feeder, often a dedicated one, and that feeder decides the timeline. Turnkey 5 MW sites with transformers already energized come up regularly in mining markets, and they convert well to inference and edge use if the power is firm. Invariant tracks several of them across the US right now.
takeaways: 5 MW at the meter is about 3.8 MW of IT at an assumed facility-to-IT demand ratio of 1.30, roughly 32 AI racks at 120 kW, or 2,300 GPUs.
Expect medium-voltage distribution service, often a dedicated 12 to 35 kV feeder and several pad-mounted transformers.
Turnkey mining sites at 5 MW can be live immediately. Check whether the rate is interruptible before you plan an uptime promise around it.
Land: 1 to 5 acres covers most layouts, more if you add generators and cooling yards.

sections.heading: What 5 MW actually fits

blocks.text: The utility serves total facility load, including cooling and electrical losses. Confirm the simultaneous loads at the site’s design conditions. At an assumed facility-to-IT demand ratio of 1.30, a 5 MW site leaves about 3.8 MW for IT. At about 120 kW per NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 rack, that is up to 32 full racks in the arithmetic example, before allowing for separate networking and storage. Air-cooled designs at 30 to 50 kW per rack fit more racks and fewer GPUs per MW. Typical buyers at this size are an inference cluster, a regional colocation room, an enterprise build or a mining expansion.

Immediate for energized turnkey sites. New service commonly runs 9 to 24 months where a feeder extension or substation bay is needed.
Contract demand on the bill, the utility one-line diagram, transformer ratings, a written statement of feeder headroom, and the rate schedule (firm or curtailable).

sections.heading: Why 5 MW sites move fast or not at all

blocks.text: A single 12.47 kV distribution feeder carries roughly 8 to 12 MW in normal operation, and utilities rarely give one customer most of it. So a new 5 MW load often means a dedicated feeder from the substation, a new breaker position or a new circuit, and each of those has its own queue and equipment lead time.
That is why energized 5 MW sites trade at a premium. The value is in the transformers and the feeder that are already there, with the utility already billing the account.

sections.heading: Converting a 5 MW mining site to AI or inference

blocks.text: Mining sites at this size have the power and usually the airflow. What they lack is redundancy, backup generation and a building that meets an enterprise tenant’s checklist. Budget for UPS, generators, fire protection and either liquid cooling or a new hall. Keep the utility service and the land; plan to rebuild most of the rest. sections.heading: How much IT load does 1 GW support?

blocks.text: Start with the measurement boundary. The utility studies the load it will serve. The owner or tenant sizes how much of that load the servers, storage and network equipment can use. Power usage effectiveness (PUE) measures the ratio of facility energy to IT energy. For early planning, a design ratio of 1.30 applied at the same operating point gives about 769 MW of IT load from 1,000 MW at the facility. For the utility request, use the engineer’s peak facility load, including cooling and electrical losses at design conditions. Annual PUE figures describe energy over a year and cannot establish peak demand.

sections.heading: How is a gigawatt-scale AI campus powered?

blocks.text: A gigawatt-scale AI campus can draw from the utility grid, dedicated on-site generation, or both. The first operating phase often uses a smaller block than the eventual campus. Identify how much reaches the facility meter by date and which equipment, interconnection work, and fuel or utility commitments support that phase.

Taylor Technology Campus illustrates the steps for an on-site generation plan. The developers targeted first power for the first half of 2028. The city agreement separately sets deadlines for the land, annexation and reclaimed-water improvements. Confirm which milestone gates the first building before using the power target to plan occupancy.

sections.heading: How ERCOT and Texas permits affect delivery

blocks.text: Texas’s adopted 16 TAC §25.194 sets interconnection requirements for covered projects on ERCOT. For customers that had yet to energize when the rule took effect, it covers new interconnections at 75 MW or more, specified expansions and certain co-location arrangements with generation. Ask the serving utility which agreement, study and financial security apply to your phase. An existing connection also warrants a utility review when the tenant, load profile or planned demand changes.

ERCOT’s November 5 Batch Zero update identified gaps in site-control evidence, long-lead equipment orders and posted security. ERCOT scheduled its report to the Public Utility Commission for December 10, 2026. Ask for the project’s latest classification and any outstanding conditions. The report date is a regulatory milestone. Each project has its own path to service.

For a site in Batch Zero, ask whether its voltage ride-through review is complete and which quarterly stability assessment it expects to enter. ERCOT showed tentative windows for initial energization in Q4 2027 and Q1 2028. Check the specific point of interconnection, phase and MW against the provider’s written approval and schedule.

In its October 19 response to the governor’s September directive, the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality said it had paused issuing permits to build or develop infrastructure directly supporting data centers and was screening pending applications for coverage. Check the status and scope of the specific permits tied to your construction plan, including any required air, water and stormwater authorizations.

description: Find a site for an AI data center or GPU cluster in the US: power density, liquid cooling, MW per GPU, firm power and the AI-ready sites Invariant has available now.
intro: An AI data center site has to deliver more power to less floor space than any facility before it. A single NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 rack draws about 120 kW and needs liquid cooling. What changes for site selection is the power: AI tenants need firm service, a fast ramp and room to grow, often from tens of MW to hundreds. Invariant matches AI buyers to sites with documented power, from energized 10 MW inference sites to a 1.5 GW campus.
takeaways: A GB200 NVL72 rack draws about 120 kW. 1,000 GPUs need roughly 2 MW at the meter including cooling.
AI tenants need firm power. Curtailable mining rates do not work for most AI contracts.
Plan for liquid cooling and heat rejection outdoors; land per MW falls less than rack density suggests.
Invariant lists AI-ready sites from 10 MW inference to 1.5 GW training campuses.

sections.heading: Power per GPU

blocks.text: At about 120 kW per 72-GPU rack, each GPU draws roughly 1.7 kW at the rack. Add cooling and power losses at a PUE of 1.3 and 1,000 GPUs need about 2.2 MW at the meter. A 100,000 GPU cluster needs over 200 MW. Training and inference differ: inference fits in 5 to 50 MW sites near users, training wants hundreds of MW in one place.

sections.heading: Firm power and redundancy

blocks.text: Many energized sites on the market were built for bitcoin mining on interruptible rates. AI tenants usually need firm service with backup. Read the power contract before pricing a conversion, and budget for generators, UPS and a second feed where the tenant requires them.

sections.heading: Cooling and land

blocks.text: Liquid cooling shrinks the building per MW but still rejects heat outside through dry coolers or towers. Substations and cooling yards scale with MW, so an AI campus still needs roughly 0.7 to 2 MW per gross acre.

faqs.question: Can I buy a data center development project with contracted power?
faqs.answer: Yes. Identify what the buyer acquires, such as land and a related service agreement or an entity holding the lease and power contracts. Review the consent, utility construction payments, and energization conditions for each phase. Valley Oasis had 29 MW of contract demand when it sold, with construction and transformer work still required.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a powered shell and a turnkey data center?
faqs.answer: A powered shell generally provides the building and access to power and connectivity, with fit-out left to the occupant. A turnkey property includes installed operating infrastructure. Confirm which systems are included and the critical IT capacity the property can deliver.

faqs.question: Does buying an energized site give the buyer immediate use of its power?
faqs.answer: Review the purchase and service documents for control of the existing service and any conditions on transfer. AIB’s DFW1 filing is an example of energized service whose economic benefit temporarily remained with the seller. Separately confirm the load and commissioning requirements for the intended use.

faqs.question: What does Tier III mean?
faqs.answer: Tier III is Uptime Institute’s concurrently maintainable classification. Verify which certificate was issued for the facility and which design or built infrastructure it covers.

faqs.question: How do I get matching sites from Invariant?
faqs.answer: Book a call or call (628) 220-8972 with your MW, states and energize-by date. We send matching sites, including off-market ones.

title: Data center site selection checklist and criteria
description: Evaluate data center sites against 12 criteria. Compare utility power and service dates by phase with a workbook and get an RFP template for site diligence.
intro: Start with the opening date and peak facility load at the utility meter for each phase. Then check usable land, site control, water, fiber and permits against that same schedule. The 12 criteria below help you shortlist sites, compare the evidence and give sellers or consultants a clear set of requirements.
takeaways: Write down IT load, facility MW at the meter, and the last acceptable service date for each phase.
Check the utility connection, land and approval path in parallel. Record which event could move the opening date.
Before paying for a land option, confirm what the serving utility accepts as proof of site control and when engineering payments come due.
Before the land option expires, compare the date the utility can support with the last day you can start commissioning.

guideActions.label: Use the site selection RFP template

sections.heading: 12 data center site selection criteria

blocks.text: Use the Excel workbook to compare power by phase and track the other site checks. Replace the two illustrative sites with your own. The workbook calculates the MW and days to spare when a cited study or service record gives comparable figures. It flags gaps when a seller quotes power without a utility record, when a required date is missing, or when the record falls short. Use the CSV for a blank checklist.

blocks.label: Download the data center site comparison workbook

columns: What you need to clear it
rows: Peak coincident facility MW at the meter, IT MW, each load step, required service date, and reliability target.
Engineering and commercial teams agree on one dated demand schedule.
Named serving utility and point of connection, with the current letter, study, service agreement, or metered records.
The document covers this site and identifies the applicable MW, phase, and status.
Utility or engineering study for the site, with assumptions, relevant outages, limiting equipment, and upgrades.
Each phase has a feasible service path and unresolved dependencies are named.
Applicable tariff and draft terms covering study fees, construction contributions, security, minimum bills, and any curtailment.
The financial model includes ramp risk and assigns each material payment.
Parcel IDs, seller authority, current options, survey, title, access for construction and equipment delivery, and routes for utility and fiber easements.
The site and required corridors can be secured within the diligence window. Identify the route and approvals needed to deliver major equipment to the pad.
Planning staff response, zoning map and ordinance, applicable restrictions, application ID, next hearing or decision, and any separate substation case.
The approval path and the expected decision dates fit the proposed construction and service schedule.
Concept plan over slope and setbacks, grading and earthwork quantities, geotechnical findings, drainage, and temporary access and staging.
Each phase and expansion area fits, earthwork is priced, and approvals due before grading are identified.
Flood mapping, wetland screening, prior use records, environmental assessment, and any recorded land-use controls.
The plan accounts for exclusions and assigns fieldwork or agency confirmation where needed.
Cooling water balance at design conditions, provider response, fire flow, sewer capacity, and any discharge limits.
The proposed cooling and fire protection can operate within documented supply and discharge constraints.
A carrier quote for each circuit with the service address, building entrance, remote handoff, capacity and install date. Request latency to your target networks.
The required circuits can be installed on time. Where two independent paths are required, verify shared segments and confirm the surviving circuit can carry the required load.
Permit register keyed to equipment, construction, and operations, with responsible agencies, dependencies, and lead times.
The schedule includes the permits needed before construction and before operation.
Dated evidence log, owners and due dates for open questions, estimated costs, and milestones for the land and power agreements.
The decision records why the site advances, stays on hold, or is ruled out.

blocks.text: Public wetland maps help screen for potential conflicts. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service describes its inventory as mapping biological extent. Confirm the method, the field boundary, and the relevant agency process before treating a mapped area as buildable.

items.label: Compare utility study fees, financial security and billing demand
Find the utility that serves a candidate site
Find the recorded agreement for an access or utility corridor
Verify whether a carrier can deliver two independent fiber circuits

sections.heading: Compare two data center sites by utility power and service date

blocks.text: Set the first phase’s facility load, opening date, and commissioning time. Enter each site’s MW and earliest service date from the utility record for that phase. Check land control, approvals, water, and fiber before advancing a site.

In this example, a 40 MW first phase must open on June 30, 2028. With 45 calendar days for commissioning, utility service must start by May 16. Site A has a seller’s 100 MW estimate and needs a utility record. Site B’s preliminary study lists 50 MW from June 15. That is 10 MW above the requirement and 30 days past the service deadline. Ask the utility about an earlier service date and check when the remaining easement can close.

sections.heading: How the data center site selection process works

blocks.text: Decide which requirements can rule out a site. For a latency-sensitive deployment, start with the latency to the networks you need to reach. For a campus with evaporative cooling, check peak-day water supply against the equipment design. Compare sites on the same phase, opening date and reliability requirements.

columns: What to bring to the next decision
rows: Specify IT load, facility MW, dates by phase, required reliability, cooling design, and network needs.
A demand schedule with the meter location or service area, design assumptions, and deadlines.
Find the serving utilities and plot the site layout, usable ground, access, flood and wetland constraints, fiber entrances, and any crossing.
A boundary and concept plan that show where evidence is strong, which sites fall short, and which constraints need an inquiry.
Verify the schedule with the parties involved
Ask the utility and planning authority which connection, upgrades, permits, and hearings apply. Check the dates for customer construction and commissioning as well.
A dated schedule showing when each workstream can finish and which dependency can hold the phase.
Compare the sites that can work
Compare the all-in cost and obligations, including the utility tariff, upgrades, water, taxes, and options for future expansion.
A shortlist with open conditions, the person responsible for each, and the evidence due before a binding commitment.

blocks.text: Give each candidate a decision and a reason. Use the actual source and phase that drove the decision. In the worked land-option example below, a preliminary study shows 50 MW for a 40 MW first phase. The earliest studied service date is still 31 days too late, so the site stays on hold while the team checks the upgrade and easement.

items: Advance to detailed diligence when the available evidence supports a viable path for every required first-phase condition. Record which studies, approvals and service terms are still due.
Hold when an open issue could change the decision. Name the party who can resolve it, the specific record you need and the deadline before the next payment or commitment.
Rule out the site for this scope when the evidence shows a fixed requirement cannot be met by the deadline. Record the threshold the site missed and what would have to change to reconsider it.

sections.heading: Data center site selection RFP template

blocks.text: Give every seller or site-selection firm the same opening date, load schedule and siting requirements. Ask for one response per proposed property and one row per power phase. A useful response ties each claim to a dated record, shows what that record covers, and names who can resolve any open conditions.

blocks.label: Download the editable site selection RFP template

rows: Street address, parcel IDs and offered boundary. Identify the owner or authorized seller, purchase or lease terms, option expiration and any off-site rights needed.
Facility load and service dates by phase

Facility MW at the meter, utility, candidate delivery point and earliest documented service date for each phase. Attach the relevant letter, study, agreement or metering record. List limits, upgrades and commercial obligations.
A dated concept plan showing building and equipment pads, setbacks, flood or wetland exclusions, access and utility corridors. Give usable acres after exclusions and state how you calculated them.
Expected demand at design conditions, the proposed providers, the service and discharge points, and written capacity or service terms where available.
Carrier and installation date for each proposed circuit. Mark building entries and any shared route segments. State which endpoints the latency estimate uses.
Jurisdiction, zoning and permit path, decision or docket references, and the next action. State which conditions must clear before land commitment, grading, utility service or operation.

blocks.text: Use the same date and unit on every bid. For the 40 MW first phase above, request service by May 16, 2028. A study showing 50 MW on June 15 still misses that schedule. Keep it on hold while the utility reviews an earlier date, and mark a seller estimate as a lead until you have a utility record.

Ask which documents the utility will require next. Dominion Energy Virginia’s transmission delivery-point criteria, effective April 1, 2026, call for a preliminary electrical diagram and scaled site plan at request intake. At the feasibility stage for a data center, they call for a 30% site plan and a local zoning conformance letter. Include the time to prepare those documents in the schedule for a site served through that process.

items.label: Compare candidate dates and power evidence

sections.heading: Data center site visit checklist

blocks.text: Bring the latest survey, title exception map and a dated plan for the first phase. Walk the proposed entrance, building and equipment pads, drainage outlet and utility routes with the civil lead and landowner’s representative. Mark each concern on the plan with a photo ID, the visit date and the team that will verify it. Bring the required opening date so the team can flag anything that could push it back.

rows: Drive the approach. Mark tight turns, overhead lines, culverts, narrow shoulders and any shared entrance on the proposed delivery route.
Ask the carrier to test the turn with the actual trailer. Have the road authority and title team confirm the approvals and access rights.
Walk the corners of the proposed pads. Photograph slope breaks, retaining walls, old slabs and overhead crossings that could change the layout.
Have the survey and civil teams check elevations. Ask geotechnical engineers where borings are needed for the foundations and equipment pads.
Follow the low ground toward the planned discharge point. Mark ditches, standing water and any off-site segment of the proposed route.
Check the drainage area, flood mapping and wetland delineation. Confirm who controls the outfall and whether a drainage easement is needed.
Mark where the candidate power route reaches the site and where crews would reach the utility equipment during construction and operation.
Ask the utility to confirm the delivery point, access requirements, corridor and dated MW by phase. Send the surveyor any route that crosses another tract.
From permitted access points, note visible handholes, valves and potential crossings. Mark where proposed utility routes share a road, bridge or trench.
Ask carriers to confirm route diversity and the water provider to confirm where it can serve the campus and on what terms.
Photograph nearby homes or other sensitive uses from the site. Mark the proposed generator and cooling yards and the planned screening between them.
Have the civil and acoustic teams check setbacks, sound limits and screening against the current plan and approval conditions.

blocks.text: At DataBank’s Orangeburg site in New York, the Phase 1 filing shows the route to the existing substation alongside the new equipment yard and detention basin. It calls for keeping that access open and identifies which transformer and generator pads are for later buildout. During a walk, trace the utility’s approach on the drawing and check which road and yard work the first phase needs. Ask the utility and civil lead to confirm any planned changes to the route.

Debrief against the same first-phase plan. For each issue, name the person responsible, the record or revised drawing they need to return, and the date it is due. If a route changes, update the land required, the easements and the construction schedule together.

sections.heading: What goes into data center site preparation?

blocks.text: Start with the civil plan for the first phase. Plot the building pads, substation and cooling yards, then add the temporary haul roads, staging areas, utility trenches, and stormwater controls needed to build them. Give the contractor the same grading assumptions and limits of disturbance that the civil engineer uses for the approval package.

rows: Ask for grading limits, quantities of soil to excavate or place as fill, the expected import or export volume, and haul routes.
Get borings and geotechnical recommendations for each major pad. Confirm the required finished elevation, unsuitable material, and how the engineer will accept the prepared ground.
Show temporary drainage, erosion controls, the route and receiving point for any dewatering, and permanent ponds or treatment areas. Include work outside the parcel boundary.
List the grading, wetland or stormwater approvals that apply, the plan revision each one covers, and the conditions the contractor must satisfy before disturbing ground.

blocks.text: The October 2025 study for the 22.31-acre Pittsburg Data Hub in California estimated that about 29,500 cubic yards of material would leave the site and that the deepest cuts could reach 15 feet. Those figures came from preliminary grading drawings. The final mitigation program called for a geotechnical and geohazard report to the city before final design approval and the start of grading and construction.

The California Energy Commission’s approval addressed the backup generating facility’s exemption. Check the local civil approvals for the actual grading scope and contractor start date. For construction stormwater, EPA says qualifying discharges generally need permit coverage at one acre of disturbance, including smaller pieces of a common plan that reaches one acre. Count connected work and check the rules with the permitting authority.

Check stormwater, dewatering and utility approvals
Read on-site boring records before estimating grading work

sections.heading: How ground conditions can change a data center construction schedule

blocks.text: Ask the geotechnical engineer to review the current grading plan, building footprints and equipment loads together. A flood design can raise the pads, adding weight that compresses the soil below. Have the engineer identify which areas must be monitored or treated and what evidence lets the contractor start foundations.

For San José Data Center 04, the December 2020 geotechnical report modeled up to 10 feet of added fill in the building areas and up to 3 feet at the substation. The same 10 feet produced different settlement estimates for the two buildings. The figures below describe the fill scenarios in that report.

blocks.text: Terracon proposed early fill placement and surveys at least monthly to confirm when foundations could begin. The table excludes settlement from structural loads and liquefaction. Ask which observations and acceptance criteria apply under the final design before adding a waiting period to the construction schedule.

The applicant’s July 2025 revision expected grading without imported fill and proposed building piles extending about 80 feet below existing grade. It also described leaving grades low on roughly the western third of the property so that shallow floodwater could pass through. Use the revised civil and foundation documents to confirm current quantities, contractor scope and the schedule before exercising a land option.

sections.heading: Can a substation transformer reach the site?

blocks.text: Check the delivery route before committing to a substation layout. Ask the equipment supplier and carrier for the loaded vehicle’s dimensions, gross weight, axle loads and axle spacing. Trace the trip from origin to pad. Check each restricted bridge, tight turn and overhead clearance, plus the last turn through the site gate. Put road work, access approvals and the move itself on the same schedule as utility energization.

The Deschutes solar and battery project’s Oregon siting application includes a field survey and turn simulations for transformer delivery. The engineer compared three routes from the Port of Portland and identified conditions that could affect the construction schedule. Oregon’s November update says the preliminary application was still under review.

columns: What to verify on your site
rows: The preferred route would likely need a bypass at the I-84 and OR 197 interchange. The modeled transformer transporter could not make the turn safely as drawn.
Have the carrier check the full turn with the actual transport configuration and get any bypass or road work into the schedule.
The survey flagged an OR 216 bridge for early investigation and called for bridge and culvert analysis after carrier selection.
Have the road authority review the specific axle loads, axle spacing and crossings before relying on the route.
Last leg to the transformer pad
Modifying the existing driveway would require about 2,700 feet of new roadway. The engineer proposed a new driveway and about 800 feet of new road instead.
Put the gate, pad, access rights, road works and construction dates on the same plan.

blocks.text: Start the road permit inquiry before setting an equipment delivery date. In Texas, TxDMV instructs applicants to submit a superheavy single-trip application three to four weeks before the permit is needed unless an approved route is already on file. The interval allows for route approval and any bridge or pavement analysis. Confirm the route, local permits and movement window with the authorities responsible for the roads you will use.

Check site access and utility delivery together

items.label: Verify freight routes and site access
Check power timing against the opening date

sections.heading: Can 40 MW of service support a 30 MW IT load?

blocks.text: Start by adding the IT, cooling and other electrical loads that can occur together. In this illustrative test, the 30 MW IT load stays fixed. Cooling rises by 3 MW at the hot-day design condition, enough to exhaust the margin on a 40 MW service.

rows: 30 MW IT + 5 MW cooling + 4 MW other
30 MW IT + 8 MW cooling + 4 MW other

blocks.text: Power usage effectiveness (PUE) compares energy over a reporting period. The service question calls for the maximum coincident demand. Ask the design engineer for that number at the utility’s meter, including cooling at the site’s design weather, power conversion losses and other site loads. Before pricing an option around 40 MW, confirm a cooling design or IT limit that fits the service, or ask the utility to study the higher requirement.

sections.heading: How to compare sites for a 40 MW first phase and an 80 MW campus

blocks.text: Consider a hypothetical project that needs 40 MW of facility power by June 2028 and 80 MW in total by June 2030. Compare the evidence for each deadline before assigning the next round of diligence.

rows: Broker quotes 100 MW based on nearby transmission. No utility connection point or date in the evidence file.
No separate expansion study or provider schedule.
Hold. Ask the serving utility to identify a study path for the first phase.
A preliminary utility study identifies a 50 MW service plan by June 2028, subject to a substation upgrade and an easement.
The study covers the first phase. Full-buildout service is still open.
Advance first-phase diligence. Confirm the easement, upgrade scope, service terms, and a study for the full campus.

blocks.text: Put the last acceptable opening date next to the expected completion dates for utility service, the customer substation, permits, and commissioning. Run the sequence of dependencies for each phase. For example, a June utility service date can still miss a June opening when commissioning follows energization. Identify which party can confirm each date and review how any open dependency affects the land decision.

Read the utility letter, study, and service agreement
Check hourly heat and humidity for the proposed cooling design
Test whether each building phase fits the tract
Compare filed acreage, utility demand and delivered IT capacity near 100 MW

sections.heading: What do utilities require before studying a data center site?

blocks.text: Consider an 80 MW facility request at three candidate sites. Keep the location, requested date and load by phase together, then check what each serving utility needs to accept the application. The land rights, engineering work and cash needed at that point differ by utility.

rows: Apply in PowerClerk with the specific location, load ramp and final load. Ohio Power requires control of the property through ownership, a lease or an option.
An 80 MW request falls in the $50,000 one-time study fee bracket, payable within 45 days under the published process.

The transmission queue application calls for an executed deed, lease or purchase option, an electrical one-line and site plan stamped by a Pennsylvania-licensed engineer, and a 120-month load ramp. Add the data center questionnaire. A memorandum or document showing only intent to buy does not satisfy the published site-control requirement.

Submit the signed study agreement and a $250,000 deposit with the queue application. The deposit funds study and engineering work. The utility says unused funds are returned if the project is canceled.

Start the feasibility review with a site plan, load letter and ramp schedule. Dominion’s contracting report also calls for construction timing, meter delivery voltage and a breakdown of load by building where applicable. Confirm which land documents Dominion needs for the request.
Dominion describes a $250,000 cash payment at signing of the Engineering Letter of Agreement, after feasibility review. Additional engineering can require further payment.

blocks.text: Before the next land payment, ask the serving utility to confirm the acceptable site-control document, the name that should appear on it, the date it expects to accept a complete application and the next payment trigger. Keep those dates separate from energization. A queue position or an engineering agreement can move the study forward while the service date and upgrades remain open.

items.label: Compare study fees, deposits and financial security
See how Project Taurus kept a 50 MW planning cap separate from the utility study

sections.heading: Project Taurus shows what a 50 MW planning approval covers

blocks.text: The Colorado Springs Planning Commission capped utility use at 50 MW for Project Taurus, a proposed data center conversion at 1565 High Tech Way. City Council later postponed the appeal and required a large-load electricity study or agreement before its April 13, 2027 meeting. Treat the 50 MW as the limit in the commission’s planning decision. Keep service capacity and the energization date open until the utility supplies them.

rows: The June 11 letter records approval of the plan modification for the data center conversion on Corporate Ridge Filing No. 1, Lot 4.
The commission denied the appeals and modified the approval. Any proposal above 50 MW would return to the Planning Commission for a hearing.
City Council action on the subsequent appeals
Council voted 7–2 to postpone the hearing until April 13, 2027. Its recorded motion calls for a large-load electricity study or agreement. The docket still lists that date as of November 26.
Utility spokesperson’s update reported by Axios

The spokesperson said the developer had yet to pay for the required study or sign a service agreement. Ask for the study authorization and the utility’s written service terms before assigning a delivery date.

blocks.text: The staff report identifies tax schedule number 7326101136. Raeden’s statement refers to 1615 Garden of the Gods Road. Follow the city’s lot description and case number to keep records for the same project together when addresses differ.

Colorado Springs Utilities’ rules require a large-load application for new or expanding electric load of at least 5 MW and applicable payment at the time of the study request. The separate Industrial Service Large Load tariff describes eligibility at 10 MW of maximum demand under its billing-period rules. Ask the utility which process and tariff apply, then get written MW by phase, required upgrades, cost responsibility, and the date and conditions of service.

sections.heading: What to verify before a data center land option expires

blocks.text: Before the option decision, compare the latest acceptable utility service date with the date the utility can support in writing. Work backward from the planned opening. Leave time for equipment testing, commissioning and schedule contingency. Put the option deadline, utility date and opening on the same calendar so the acquisition team can see which evidence it needs before the next payment.

columns: What it means for the option decision
rows: 40 MW at the meter and an opening on June 30, 2028. Allow 45 calendar days for commissioning and 15 for contingency after energization.
The latest acceptable utility service date is May 1, 2028 under this schedule.
Read the dates in the power record
A preliminary utility study shows 50 MW on June 1, 2028, subject to a substation upgrade and an easement.
The studied MW exceeds the phase requirement. The service date is 31 days later than the project can accept.
Decide what needs to be on file
The illustrative land option expires October 15, 2027. The later 80 MW phase has no utility date.
Hold the acquisition decision. Ask the utility for a dated first-phase plan and the status of the upgrade and easement. Record the later phase as open.

blocks.text: For a real site, give the utility the same tract, point of service if known, and load dates the acquisition team is using. Dominion Energy Virginia starts its typical process with a site plan, load letter and load ramp schedule. faqs.question: Can raising a data center site for flood protection delay foundations?
faqs.answer: Added fill can compress underlying soil. Ask the geotechnical engineer to estimate settlement for each building and equipment pad using the current grading design, specify how to measure it, and confirm when foundations can begin. Recheck those assumptions after a grading revision.

faqs.question: What are the most important data center site selection criteria?
faqs.answer: Start with the amount of power the facility needs at the meter and the date it needs it. Then screen usable land and control, available cooling water, independent fiber paths where required, hazards, and the local approvals that could change the schedule. The order can change with the project.

faqs.question: What are the steps in data center site selection?
faqs.answer: Set your required power, reliability, and delivery dates. Screen land and infrastructure against those thresholds. Verify the utility, permit, and construction schedules for each phase, then compare costs and contractual obligations across the sites that can meet them.

faqs.question: What should you check on a data center site visit?
faqs.answer: Bring a current survey and first-phase plan. Walk the access road, pad corners, drainage outlet, and proposed power, fiber and water entries. Mark photos and any conflicts on the plan. Give each open item to the utility, surveyor, engineer or carrier who can verify it before the land option expires.

faqs.question: What does site preparation include for a data center?
faqs.answer: It includes clearing and grading, preparing the building and equipment pads, bringing in or hauling out soil, installing temporary drainage and erosion controls, and preparing access and utility corridors. Ask for quantities and permit dates for the first phase so the early civil work can be priced and scheduled.

faqs.question: What does a utility load study establish?
faqs.answer: A load study evaluates a proposed request and can identify a service plan, upgrades, and conditions for a specific site. Read the study’s assumptions alongside the subsequent service terms to see what the utility has committed to and what is still contingent.

faqs.question: Does a sewer capacity letter establish water availability for a data center?
faqs.answer: A sewer capacity letter addresses discharge to a sewer system. Obtain a separate water service commitment from the supplier for the actual withdrawal or delivery needs, including peak demand, service timing and infrastructure by phase.

faqs.question: Should you control land before requesting a data center load study?
faqs.answer: Ask the serving utility what it accepts at the study application stage. AEP Ohio accepts ownership, a lease or an option for its formal data center study requests. For Duquesne Light’s transmission queue, the published form calls for an executed deed, lease or purchase option. Its form also requires the applicant to show the relationship to the holder of the land rights when those names differ.

title: Powered Shell vs. Turnkey Data Center: Power, Fit-Out and Rent
description: Compare powered shell and turnkey data centers by utility MW, critical IT load, fit-out scope, commissioning, and rent commencement. See what to ask before you sign.
coverCaption: Illustration of a fitted data hall. The lease and acceptance documents define the equipment and capacity included in a specific delivery.
intro: A powered shell typically includes a building and a path to electrical service. The tenant takes responsibility for some or all of the interior fit-out. In a turnkey data center, the provider delivers the electrical, cooling and safety systems required to operate the contracted data hall. Before comparing quotes, get both offers in terms of the same deliverable: critical IT capacity accepted for use by a specific date.
takeaways: Ask where each MW figure is measured. Service at the meter, capacity backed by an uninterruptible power supply, and critical IT load available in a hall describe different parts of the facility.
Request the lease exhibit that assigns each piece of equipment, the acceptance test, and the date that starts rent.
Price phased deliveries separately. A campus can be under lease, drawing power, and accepting IT load in different buildings at the same time.

sections.heading: What is included in each delivery?

blocks.text: Prince William County’s assessment report describes a powered shell as a building with access to power and connectivity where the tenant completes the interior build-out. Its turnkey category covers fully built and equipped facilities. Those categories give you a starting point. Use the deal documents to assign the actual work, including who owns or removes installed fixtures when the lease expires.

rows: Confirm utility service size, delivery date and the exact point where landlord-provided equipment ends.
Confirm accepted critical IT load at the contractual handoff, by hall and delivery phase.
Assign switchgear, UPS, backup generation, cooling, controls and rack power distribution to named parties.
Check included redundancy, allowed rack density, cooling method and any tenant-specific equipment or design changes.
Check shell sign-off and the date the tenant can begin work. Track commissioning and occupancy for the finished hall separately.
Request the agreed commissioning results, occupancy evidence for the hall and signed acceptance for the capacity being delivered.
Identify which party funds and owns the fit-out, when rent begins, and whether the tenant reimburses the landlord for work.
Confirm the billable kW, delivery-by-phase terms, power charges, and which services are included in base rent.

sections.heading: A marketed 22.8 MW shell still has a delivery question

blocks.text: A Five 9s Digital brochure markets a 50,000-square-foot shell in South Carolina with 22.8 MW of near-term power. It estimates about three months from application to bringing power from a substation to the building. That describes a broker’s service estimate. Ask for the utility’s written allocation for this building, the start date of the estimate, the equipment and work on each side of the meter, and the resulting IT capacity in the proposed design.

Public records can help you find the property and establish which work was permitted. Prince William County’s data center process, for example, shows separate shell approvals, trade and fire inspections, and an option for temporary occupancy by phase. Its assessment report also estimates about 400 MW across the powered-shell inventory from floor area and a market density assumption. Use that portfolio estimate for context and ask the utility for service evidence for the actual building.

sections.heading: What changed when Lake Mariner amended its fit-out terms?

blocks.text: TeraWulf’s August 2026 presentation says July 5 amendments for buildings CB-3, CB-4 and CB-5 at Lake Mariner changed delivery timing and how tenant-requested fit-out was paid. TeraWulf said it would fund about $150 million of fit-out costs incurred through June 30 and recover the covered work through rent. It also said the tenant would pay cash, plus an agreed margin, for fit-out costs incurred after July 5. The rent comparison changes once you know who advanced the money and which costs the rent covers.

At September 30, TeraWulf reported 438 MW of contracted critical IT capacity at Lake Mariner, with 102 MW in operation and generating revenue. Its November release identified another 336 MW under construction across CB-4 and CB-5. Those records give three useful measures for a transaction review: the contracted total, the amount already operating, and the work remaining. For a specific offer, get the corresponding handoff and rent schedule by hall.

sections.heading: How do you compare two quotes per usable IT kilowatt?

blocks.text: Start with one delivery requirement, such as 8 MW of accepted critical IT load in the first phase. In an illustrative comparison, a shell priced at $75 per month per kW of 10 MW of gross building service bills $750,000 a month before fit-out and other charges. A fitted offer priced at $125 per month per kW of 8 MW of IT capacity bills $1 million a month before additional charges. Confirm the shell design can support the required 8 MW, then compare tenant capital, early rent during construction, energy and operating charges, and the date each option can carry the workload.
